Title: Measuring Foot Traffic at Open Streets and Open Newbury Street
Presenter Title: Streets Cabinet
Background Info: The City has no reliable way to count attendance at its large pedestrian-only street events, Open Streets and Open Newbury Street, or to measure how these events change everyday foot traffic in the area. Reliable counts would show the economic impact of these events and the operational capacity needed to keep them safe, accessible, and vibrant.
Question: What impact do Open Newbury and Open Streets have on foot traffic on the pedestrianized street and the surrounding area?
Outcomes: We hope to understand attendance compared with a typical non-event day, the economic impact of event foot traffic, the sources of attendees, and the street segments that draw the most attendees.
Resources: We can offer previous data collected on the event, specifically feedback surveys from both pedestrians//attendees and participating businesses.
Expertise: We seek expertise in data analytics and built environment-based economic development.

Title: Mapping Development Impact Mitigations on Boston’s Streets
Presenter Title: Transportation Demand Management Planner, Streets Cabinet
Background Info: Since the late 1980s, the City of Boston has executed hundreds of Transportation Access and Plan Agreements (TAPAs) with real estate developers and institutions to formalize traffic impact mitigations surrounding large development projects. Various efforts have been made to streamline the TAPA process—reorganizing physical files, extracting mitigation data, and integrating records into the City’s CRM platform. However, no work has been done to geolocate these committed mitigations. Since the City can maintain only a limited amount of street infrastructure annually, a mapping tool—or equivalent—that tracks external developer investments will enable informed decisions on resource allocation.
Question: When and where have developers committed to changes in street infrastructure?
Outcomes: We hope to produce a map that shows where developers have committed capital improvements within the City’s ROW, as well as a report that encapsulates cumulative improvements to street infrastructure.
Resources: We can offer physical and digital TAPAs, a formatted list of traffic impact mitigations extracted from historic TAPAs, and inventories of City-owned assets.
Expertise: We seek expertise in AI image processing and coding to extract spatial information from site plans / memos and cross-reference with existing asset databases.

Title: Developing an Information Kit on Multimodal Options for New Residents
Presenter Title: Transportation Demand Management Planner, Streets Cabinet
Background Info: According to 2024 American Community Survey estimates, nearly 20 percent of Boston’s total population changed homes, either within or from outside the city. A continued influx of new residents, combined with the City’s commitment to multimodal transportation, provides a window of opportunity to nudge people to increase sustainable transportation use. For the past three years, a program has been proposed that would provide new residents with a customizable information kit on multimodal transportation options. Despite the demonstrated need for such a resource, there has been little progress. Design and branding support would be immensely helpful.
Question: What kind of information is most valuable to new residents? What information should the City provide, in what order, and where should it be sourced from, to encourage mode shift? What funding opportunities are available that the City should tap into?
Outcomes: We hope to develop finalized resources for new residents, produced in both digital and physical formats, with branding and funding recommendations.
Resources: We can offer a draft version of the resources, translated text, and an inventory of POIs and events aggregated in 2024–2025.
Expertise: We seek expertise in cartography, graphic design, and editing / publishing.

Title: Identifying a Cyclist High Injury Network in Boston
Presenter Title: Senior Transportation Planner, Boston Streets
Background Info: Using injury crash data to identify the highest risk streets for cycling in Boston results in gaps where we have had no injury crashes. We typically use segments that are 1/2 mile long for analysis. We could go with shorter segments, but the network would be choppy. We are updating our Vision Zero Action Plan. We would like to commit to studying this question as an action item. Identifying the High Injury Network will help us prioritize safety investments.
Question: Should we seek ways to have a more cohesive High Injury Network (HIN) for cyclists? If so, what data might help us do this?
Outcomes: We hope to develop a clear rationale for how we define our cycling HIN.
Resources: We can offer the crash data used to create our draft cyclist HIN, as well as staff time to identify other relevant data sources.
Expertise: We seek expertise in data analysis and visualization, along with knowledge of potential sources of data related to bike safety.

Title: Communicating the Hidden Costs of Urban Vehicle Ownership
Presenter Title: Director of Parking & Curb Management, Streets Cabinet
Background Info: New Boston residents frequently default to private cars because they underestimate the hidden financial and time costs of urban vehicle ownership. While the City has invested heavily in expanding the supply of sustainable transit alternatives, there remains a critical gap in demand-side behavioral tools. We would like to build a digital tool that nudges residents toward multimodal transportation based on their addresses and daily habits. By visualizing the time and money saved through alternative options, this tool will directly advance the congestion and emissions reduction goals of Go Boston 2030 and the Climate Action Plan and reduce curb competition.
Question: How can we develop a data-driven, interactive "Mobility Cost & Lifestyle Calculator" that visualizes the true financial and time costs of private vehicle ownership for residents, ultimately demonstrating the benefits of sustainable, multimodal transportation options?
Outcomes: We hope to make Boston residents aware of the costs of private vehicle ownership and support adoption of new transportation behaviors where appropriate.
Resources: We can offer City datasets and departmental access and support.
Expertise: We seek expertise in data science / engineering, UX/UI design and behavioral economics, and urban planning and GIS.

Title: Studying the Types of Micromobility Devices on Our Streets
Presenter Title: Director of Parking & Curb Management, Streets Cabinet; Transportation Planner, Boston Transportation Department
Background Info: The Transportation Department has been taking vehicle counts across the city for over 10 years as part of the Quarterly Traffic Counts Program. The Data is published and features the number of vehicles over a 48-hour period, specifically reporting the number of bicycle users. Over the last decade, we have seen an increase in the number of bicycle users. Over the last several years, electric bicycles and other mobility devices have become more affordable, enabling more people to commute by bike, scooter, or other electric device. We would like to research the composition of the commuting fleet.
Question: What kind of micromobility vehicles are using Boston streets, and what percentage of total micromobility users do they make up? How do these data inform design and policy?
Outcomes: We hope to create a report defining a more specific breakdown of vehicles, in particular micromobility vehicles, and uses (commercial / private) that operate on our streets.
Resources: We can offer agency staff time for study time and analysis work.
Expertise: We seek expertise in traffic data collection and processing.

Title: Piloting Public Art at Boston Bus Stops
Presenter Title: Transit Team Director, Boston Transportation Department
Background Info: Boston has nearly 2,000 bus stops, among the most-used public spaces in the city, but many offer a limited waiting experience and do little to reflect their neighborhoods. With major investment in new bus shelters coming, the City needs a replicable framework for neighborhood-focused public art that maintains accessibility, durability, and transit operations.
Question: How can Boston build a scalable, equitable public art program at bus stops that supports local artists, reflects neighborhood identity, and improves the rider experience?
Outcomes: We hope to develop a framework for a 10- to 20-stop pilot: peer-city models, art formats, site and artist selection, community engagement, costs, maintenance, roles, and funding.
Resources: We can support with management, oversight, and direction of the overall program in partnership with other city departments.
Expertise: We seek expertise in public art, public space, and transportation, ideally with experience building art programs for transit or civic infrastructure.

Title: Predicting Pavement Condition for Asphalt Resurfacing Prioritization
Presenter Title: DoIT Citywide Analytics Team
Background Info: The City spends over $40 million a year on roadway resurfacing and reconstruction. We are currently investing in pavement condition mapping using LIDAR that provides us with a temporal snapshot of roadway conditions. Given the pace of annual utility excavations, the mapped street conditions will quickly become outdated. However, the causes of road degradation are well known and include traffic, weather, and utility excavations, for which we have robust data. We would like to create a model that predicts pavement condition in intermediate years between detailed measurement campaigns to be used to inform decisions in resurfacing prioritization.
Question: How can we use our existing data to predict pavement condition? Can we predict today, one month from now, and six months from now?
Outcomes: We hope to produce a data pipeline and ML model that we can run during Asphalt Resurfacing Program planning.
Resources: We can offer data on traffic, weather, freeze / thaw cycles, and excavation square footage. Also, the City is currently collecting LIDAR data for ground truth.
Expertise: We seek expertise in building and testing machine learning models.

Title: Designing a Public Competition to Improve T Predictions
Presenter Title: Deputy Director of Software Engineering, MBTA
Background Info: Nearly a million riders a day plan trips using our departure predictions in Google/Apple Maps, on our website, and using our app. Our predictions are about 80% accurate… about 80% of the time. Accuracy drops at terminals, and during service disruptions, when riders need it most. The industry benchmark for prediction accuracy counts every prediction the same, so better scores don’t necessarily mean better trips for riders. We want to run a public machine-learning competition on our open data, scored in a way that rewards improvements that matter the most to riders.
Question: How should we structure a transit prediction competition to maximize the value of our predictions to riders?
Outcomes: We hope to develop a (1) ready-to-launch competition, including test datasets and submission criteria; (2) scoring method that better centers impacts on riders.
Resources: We can offer our archives of real-time vehicle locations, operational schedules, and service alerts, plus current predictions and staff time with our predictions team.
Expertise: We seek expertise in forecast evaluation or transit rider behavior, as well as experience designing ML competitions.

Title: Developing a System to Coordinate Community Hypertension Screening
Presenter Title: Chronic Disease Prevention and Control, BPHC
Background Info: Boston’s Live Long and Well Population Health Equity Agenda highlights the importance of screening for cardiometabolic conditions early so they can be successfully managed. Hypertension is a major risk factor to developing heart disease, stroke and diabetes. Offering free blood pressure screening in our communities is an effective way to screen for hypertension. Many healthcare and community-based organizations offer community screenings and there is not one city-wide schedule / dashboard for finding out where they are. A tool will reduce the barriers for residents by providing a central list of where they can get a free screening, even without insurance.
Question: Is it feasible to build an online tool and map that auto-updates from multiple healthcare and community-based organization calendars? Is there a better way to do this?
Outcomes: We hope to develop a prototype for an online tool and map that provides a central list of where residents can get a blood pressure screening.
Resources: We can offer the City website database.
Expertise: We seek expertise in development of tools and dashboards and an understanding of IT systems across organizations.

Title: Translating Population Health Data into Community Tools
Presenter Title: Health of Boston Program Director, BPHC
Background Info: The City’s Health of Boston (HOB) reports make important population health data publicly available, but traditional report formats may not always meet the needs of community members, organizations and other users. There is limited systematic information about how people currently use these data, what information or formats are missing, and which approaches would make findings easier to understand and act on. This project would help ensure that HOB products are designed around user needs rather than assuming that publication alone makes data accessible or useful.
Question: What do stakeholders need from HOB data, and what new products would best fit those needs?
Outcomes: We hope to identify and engage diverse HOB users to understand what would make the data more useful, then develop and test new interfaces or tools such as neighborhood summaries, interactive fact sheets, and data visualizations.
Resources: We can offer existing HOB products, brand guidelines, access to HOB super users, and relevant data and analyses.
Expertise: We seek expertise in human-centered design / user research, data visualization, and public health data translation.

Title: Mapping Neighborhood Health Indices to Guide Public Health Investment
Presenter Name: Johnna Murphy, Aanchal Gupta, Tibrine da Fonseca, & Sanouri Ursprung
Presenter Title: Boston Public Health Commission
Background Info: To support Boston’s Live Long and Well Population Health Equity Agenda, BPHC seeks to strengthen how we identify and map drivers of inequities and social determinants of health (SDOH) within neighborhoods. Resource allocation across the city requires understanding need across multiple dimensions of wellness and opportunity, ranging from morbidity or mortality, to social determinants of health like community conditions and economic opportunity. This pilot will review existing geographic SDOH and equity indices, assess their applicability to Boston, and identify which provide meaningful geographic distinctions to guide programming and investment.
Question: How can existing equity measures, alone or layered, define need across multiple dimensions of health to inform resource allocation across Boston?
Outcomes: We hope to develop a tested framework for measuring geographic inequities integrating SDOH dimensions beyond mortality outcomes, and an interactive atlas prototype identifying where needs and assets concentrate.
Resources: We can offer census, health surveillance and public SDOH data, such as food access, transportation, and green space.
Expertise: We seek expertise in spatial epidemiology, equity measurement, small-area analysis, resource prioritization, and geographic visualization.

Title: Mapping Heat Vulnerability Across Boston
Presenter Name: Roy Wada, Johnna Murphy, Tibrine da Fonseca, Tom Fitzgerald, Leon Bethune, Aanchal Gupta, & Sanouri Ursprung
Presenter Title: BPHC
Background Info: Boston’s climate-related health risks are not experienced evenly across neighborhoods, and existing data systems do not always capture how heat exposure intersects with health and social conditions. Building on and combining existing heat initiatives, including Common SENSES sensors on Blue Hill Avenue, this project would assess how neighborhood-level heat exposure intersects with health outcomes and broader structural conditions. It would also review existing Social Determinants of Health (SDOH) indices to identify approaches most relevant to Boston and strengthen local heat-risk assessment and future place-based analyses to align with Climate Action Plan strategies.
Question: Can neighborhood heat, health and SDOH data improve local monitoring and help guide long-term mitigation and communication?
Outcomes: We hope to create heat vulnerability and illness maps, identify mitigation priorities, and create communication products. We also hope to establish reusable approaches for quantifying and visualizing climate / SDOH data and integrating into other health priorities.
Resources: We can offer analytical support, partner coordination, aggregated ESSENCE ED and 311 data, Common SENSES sensors, and airport sensors.
Expertise: We seek expertise in urban climate, spatial epidemiology, and equitable heat mitigation.

Title: Identifying Multi-Year Trends in the Farmers Market Coupon Program
Presenter Title: Farmers Market Manager, Office of Food Justice
Background Info: The Farmers Market Coupon Program (FMCP) increases fresh food access for food-insecure Boston residents while directing municipal purchasing power to local farms and neighborhood markets. While the program successfully distributes thousands of dollars in coupons annually, critical questions remain regarding equity, participant mobility, and long-term utilization. In 2026, OFJ upgraded its application intake process to capture participant-level demographic indicators, as well as issued surveys capturing participant experience. OFJ now possesses rich quantitative datasets but requires academic research support to conduct spatial econometrics and cross-tabular demographic analyses.
Question: How have FMCP redemption patterns and geographic shopping flows evolved, and how do participant demographic characteristics (income, age, household size, SNAP status, home ZIP code) and personal experience influence coupon utilization across Boston's neighborhood farmers markets?
Outcomes: We hope to develop a report that identifies trends in coupon redemption that will inform future improvements to the program.
Resources: We can offer multi-year redemption data, 2026 participant intake data, participant feedback, and staff / market interviews.
Expertise: We seek expertise in data visualization and quantitative/qualitative data analysis.

Title: Gathering Data to Close the Summer Meals Gap
Presenter Title: Deputy Director, Office of Food Justice
Background Info: During the school year, BPS serves free meals to all students. In summer, federal rules for open Summer Eats sites require on-site, fixed-time, mostly cold meals at far fewer locations. Food insecurity among families with school-aged children persists, yet Summer Eats attendance stays low. Without data on how families fill the gap, the City cannot target outreach or reallocate food resources.
Question: How do food-insecure families in Dorchester, Roxbury, East Boston, and Mattapan meet nutritional needs in summer, and what keeps them from Summer Eats sites?
Outcomes: We hope to develop a family food survey sent through ParentSquare, and an action plan for OFJ, BCYF, and BPS on-site placement, and messaging.
Resources: We can offer multi-year redemption data, and staff / program manager interviews.
Expertise: We seek expertise in survey design and quantitative methods, with experience drafting, translating, and analyzing municipal or school family surveys.

Theme: Government Operations, Data, and Digital Services
Title: Digitizing the City’s Vital Records
Presenter Title: Registrar, Registry Department
Background Info: The City of Boston manages vital records dating back to the 1600’s. These early records were written in goatskin vellum. 400 years later, while society operates in a digital world, the Registry issues and stores records on paper. Each year, the Registry issues over 100,000 copies of birth, death, and marriage records to constituents and we have millions of records which have yet to be digitized at all. How can the City move our most vital records into the digital era? And promote access to records digitally in a way that is useful for constituents?
Question: Can we automatically transcribe vital information from physical books into an electronic database? Can Boston issue digital vital records?
Outcomes: We hope to have Digital Certified Birth, Death, and Marriage Certificates as easily searchable vital records that reduce thousands of hours of staff and constituent time.
Resources: We can offer existing electronic database, access to old vital records, clerk time and expertise, and quality assurance support.
Expertise: We seek expertise in machine learning and AI, digital security, legal and policy expertise related to government ID programs

Theme: Government Operations, Data, and Digital Services
Title: Enabling Online Marriage Intention Appointments
Presenter Title: Registrar, Registry Department
Background Info: You can buy a house, meet the love of your life, and even make court appearances online. But, in Massachusetts, you have to appear in person at City Hall to get a marriage license. Boston’s Registry facilitates over 6,000 marriage intentions yearly—each one in person. Thousands of survey results collected by the Registry from constituents indicate a huge demand for virtual services. Although love is hard, through this project the City can make getting married a little easier.
Question: Can we offer a remote alternative to in-person appointments that maintains the credibility and trust of an official process?
Outcomes: We hope to understand how couples and clerks could save significant time with remote appointments, and we hope for the City of Boston to develop capacity for more high-quality online services.
Resources: We can offer existing surveys, existing processes, access to the Calendly appointment system, and Boston’s research and communication with the State thus far.
Expertise: We seek expertise in cyber security, legal, service delivery and design, and process improvement.

Theme: Government Operations, Data, and Digital Services
Title: Creating an Automatic System for In-Person Service Evaluation
Presenter Title: Manager of Continuous Improvement, Election Department
Background Info: The City of Boston gives out over 20,000 birth, death, and marriage certificates in-person each year. While the Registry has a wealth of data about online transactions, it wants to evaluate its in-person service levels for process improvement purposes. The Registry has tried taking data manually and adding an electronic ordering system, but they took too much staff time and reduced service quality, respectfully. Automatically tracking in-person service times is a critical step in transforming not only Registry services, but all types of in-person services that local government provides.
Question: Can we automatically track how long it takes to get an in-person certificate or service from the Registry?
Outcomes: We hope to create a product or system that will show us how long constituents wait before they start receiving services and how long those services take.
Resources: We can offer concurrent manual tracking, historical time-studies, and access to the Registry and its operational data.
Expertise: We seek expertise in computer vision models or similar systems for operational tracking.

Theme: Government Operations, Data, and Digital Services
Title: Developing a Poll Worker Training Curriculum
Presenter Title: Project Coordinator, City Records Cabinet
Background Info: The City of Boston aims to recruit, hire and train over 2,000 poll workers in preparation for yearly primary and general elections. The department wants to update its training materials and methods to account for changes in voting laws, new department procedures/systems, and a new federal landscape.  Specifically, we want to redesign our training methods, content, learning evaluation, and delivery to be more accessible and effective for our poll workers. This training should prepare them to serve constituents more efficiently, ensure statutory compliance, and reinforce trust in Boston’s elections.
Question: Can we create better outcomes for our poll workers and voters via improved training and training infrastructure?
Outcomes: We hope to develop an improved poll worker experience, with reduced mistakes and remedial trainings, improved retention, and reduced phone calls to the Election Department on Election Day.
Resources: We can offer access to our current training systems, our current training slides and resources, Clerk’s Books, Poll Worker committee groups, and call center data.
Expertise: We seek expertise in effective teaching methods, as well as effective hybrid teaching systems.

Theme: Government Operations, Data, and Digital Services
Title: Evaluating the Impact of the Permitting Transformation Initiative
Presenter Title: Mayor’s Office of New Urban Mechanics
Background Info: The inaugural Mayor’s Permitting Transformation Initiative is launching to transform permitting so that constituents have a predictable, transparent, and efficient experience from their first touchpoint with the City through to when they achieve their outcome. On October 1, we kicked off the beta launch focused on small building permitting. The PTI is testing three levers of change: organized review stages, timeline expectations, and new dedicated permitting managers. We would like to understand if these levers of intervention lead to a more livable city: more affordable to live, more business friendly, more fun.
Question: How is the Initiative shifting permitting from a transactional, fragmented process into a predictable, constituent-centered system that enables sustainable growth for the City?
Outcomes: We hope to learn about what works in permitting transformation that can be applied to other permitting reforms—such as starting and operating a business, using or enhancing the public realm, or for hosting outdoor events.
Resources: We can offer access to live cases, permitting data from multiple agencies, ability to co-design a city-wide beta test, and staff time.
Expertise: We seek expertise in evaluating governance reform and systems change efforts.

Theme: Government Operations, Data, and Digital Services
Title: Building Boston’s Municipal AI Knowledge Engine Starting at 311
Presenter Title: Comms & Content Manager, Boston 311
Background Info: Managing a major CRM transition in a high-volume environment like Boston 311 is a massive operational lift. We already have the right pieces in place: departmental SOP ownership, our Help Center (Innovation Expo), and real-time Google Chat data. The goal now is knowledge delivery and change management. When call takers are on live calls, they have seconds to locate answers before friction builds. This friction comes from manual searches during live calls causing longer constituent wait times. An internal AI knowledge query engine would be a game-changer for 311 to index operational documentation and reduce information retrieval time.
Question: How can an internal AI query engine streamline real-time knowledge delivery for 311 call takers and establish the foundational blueprint for internal municipal AI LLMs across Boston City Hall?
Outcomes: We hope to deploy a functional, SOP-backed AI query prototype and evaluate its impact on information search speed and call handling time, in a scalable framework that other departments can adopt.
Resources: We can offer department-owned SOPs, CRM routing matrices, live user-testing, and Google Chat Q&A summaries.
Expertise: We seek expertise in NLP, RAG, and HCD for real-time operational workflows.

Theme: Government Operations, Data, and Digital Services
Title: Building Boston’s Hub Table Data and Evaluation Infrastructure
Presenter Title: Citywide Hub Coordinator, Boston Police Department
Background Info: Boston’s Hub Tables are multidisciplinary meetings between first responders, community-based organizations, and public health agencies to coordinate interventions for high-risk individual and family situations. As the model has expanded, the Hubs lack a standardized citywide method for tracking interventions and outcomes. We want to develop a data and evaluation system that helps Boston understand Hub activity, what happens after intervention, and where the model works or needs improvement. This project would also identify system-level trends, service gaps, and emerging needs among Boston residents at the highest levels of risk.
Question: How can Boston meaningfully measure the impact of Hub interventions and use that data to understand broader patterns across the city’s service system?
Outcomes: We hope to develop a standardized Hub data architecture, evaluation framework, and reporting prototype.
Resources: We can offer agency staff time, connections to community partners, opportunities to test prototypes, and access to existing data.
Expertise: We seek expertise in public sector data science, public program evaluation, and privacy standards.

Theme: Government Operations, Data, and Digital Services
Title: Developing Metrics to Understand Collective Impact of City Grantmaking
Presenter Name: Rachel Goldstein, Ryan Nicoll, & Peter Meacham
Presenter Title: Procurement Department
Background Info: In FY26, the City awarded ~$48M in grants of varying size and scope through 26 city departments to over 1,100 community partners. Departments require all grant partners to submit reports on how funds are used at grant period close. These reports do not collect standardized metrics and are not analyzed across grant programs, making it challenging to demonstrate their collective impact and community benefit. We wish to modify use-of-funds reports to collect standard qualitative and quantitative metrics to understand and evaluate grant program impact. We hope to collect this information so we can understand the story of grant programs without additional administrative burden.
Question: How do we create a reporting framework across diverse City grant programs?
Outcomes: We have standardized impact measures for City grantmaking informed by other jurisdictions and can implement these measures in FY28.
Resources: We can provide historical grantmaking data from Airtable, examples of past / current department use-of-funds forms, and examples of data collected from previous reports.
Expertise: We seek expertise in mixed-methods surveying and measurement of program performance outcomes.

Theme: Government Operations, Data, and Digital Services
Title: Evaluating Construction Project Success
Presenter Title: Asst. Director of Administration and Finance, Public Facilities
Background Info: Public Facilities manages over $100 million in capital construction projects annually. Projects include large scale renovations on public buildings (libraries, community centers, and schools), as well as smaller projects like windows or roof replacements for various municipal buildings. Our leaders recently identified a gap in our knowledge of how our stakeholders (the user agencies whose buildings we construct) would rate our success once a project is complete. We’ve identified areas where we’d like to measure our success: communication with user agency, public meetings effectiveness, and building quality (initially and after a year or two), and we’d like feedback on where we could improve.
Question: How could PFD be evaluating its’ performance in terms of effectiveness (work quality), outcomes (building quality), budget (within budget or not), and schedule (within schedule or not)?
Outcomes: We hope to develop tools for different types of evaluation, as well as a recommended plan for when and how often these tools should be used to maximize our own learning and improvement.
Resources: We can offer staff time, raw or reported process data, and connections with our user agencies / external stakeholders.
Expertise: We seek expertise in project evaluation.

Title: Finding the Bostonians the Library Isn’t Reaching
Presenter Title: Chief Communications Officer, Boston Public Library
Background Info: Boston Public Library’s current surveys only reach people who already use the library. We know little about the residents who don’t: what they need, what keeps them away, and how they hear about library services. In a time of economic uncertainty, residents need to know what the library offers, and BPL needs to spend its limited outreach resources where they matter most. A needs survey that reaches non-patrons would show which communities we are missing and where to invest.
Question: Who are we not reaching in Boston? What do they need and how can they find out about library services?
Outcomes: We hope to develop a survey design and rollout plan that reaches patrons and non-patrons. We also hope for findings on where to direct outreach.
Resources: We can offer staff time, past patron survey results, branch and circulation data, and access to branches and community partners.
Expertise: We seek expertise in survey design, sampling hard-to-reach populations, and community segmentation.

Title: Mapping Slavery in Colonial Boston
Presenter Title: City Archaeologist and Dir. of Archaeology, City Archaeology Program
Background Info: Boston’s history of slavery is poorly understood in the landscape of the city today. The Archaeology team maintains a list of people enslaved in Boston from 1630 to 1783, but where they lived and worked has not been mapped.  Researchers will use free, scanned deeds and probate records to locate enslavers’ homes and link those properties to the names of the people they enslaved.
Question: Where in Boston were enslaved people living and working? How can this data be made accessible and actionable?
Outcomes: We hope to develop a digital map (ArcGIS or QGIS) of places of enslavement in Boston.
Resources: We can offer scanned deeds and probate records, as well as staff time to train partners in both research and mapping.
Expertise: We seek expertise in detailed archival research, careful database upkeep, and citable sourcing.

Title: Creating Charging Stations for Power Wheelchairs & Mobility Scooters
Presenter Title: Commissioner, Boston Disabilities Commission
Background Info: Over 80,000 Boston residents self-identify as disabled, a majority of whom are mobility impaired. When factoring in visitors and commuters, this figure grows greatly and will only increase as our population ages. Many of those with mobility impairments use wheelchairs or scooters that run on batteries, which need to charge at regular intervals. Limited battery life impedes folks’ ability to go to medical appointments, shopping, social events, and more. They must plan every trip precisely or risk losing power and becoming stuck—literally—wherever they are. Batteries can also die unexpectedly, and there is no system to respond. People are just left on their own, hoping that someone will help them.
Question: Can we create a system of public charging stations for power wheelchairs and mobility scooters throughout the city, similar to charging stations for EVs and electric bikes?
Outcomes: We hope to develop a pilot plan for wheelchair charging stations that could be set up in BCYF Centers, libraries, or other municipal buildings that are open to the public, with a public map of the locations of these charging stations.
Resources: We can offer staff time and data on potential pilot locations.
Expertise: We seek expertise in site planning, ADA-compliant design, and spatial analysis to select pilot sites.

Title: Developing a Self-Assessment Tool for Digital Accessibility
Presenter Title: Accessibility & Inclusion Training Spec., Disabilities Commission
Background Info: The Disabilities Commission ensures compliance with Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act, providing access to all municipal programs and services. In April 2027, new regulations come into effect which address accessibility for all digital products. Due to a decentralized model of communications and content creation, over 25,000 employees will have to self-monitor for compliance with these new standards. Currently, several disparate checkers exist that may review a specific type of digital product or check a specific regulation, but they do not include resources on remediation or collect data on types of errors encountered by CoB staff.
Question: Can we create a tool that supports self-assessment for digital accessibility and training at scale?
Outcomes: We hope to develop a tool that assesses digital accessibility and supplies resources for remediation. We also hope for a dashboard created from this data to guide training efforts.
Resources: We can offer interdepartmental staff time and expertise, as well as plain language resources for remediating digital accessibility
Expertise: We seek expertise in prototyping digital tools, especially automated accessibility testing and/or user-centered tool design.

Title: Exploring Service Gaps for Returning Citizens
Presenter Title: Executive Director, Mayor’s Office of Returning Citizens
Background Info: The Mayor’s Office of Returning Citizens (ORC) exists to coordinate reentry services across partnerships and departments for anyone formerly incarcerated. Despite having many successes, services in Boston are often limited for people with multi-dimensional needs, creating gaps in services. ORC conducted a Needs Assessment in 2025 to understand the experiences of returning citizens, highlighting concerns across basic living needs. This project would build on that work, informing how current services contribute to these gaps and how to better address them.
Question: How do one-size-fits-all services fail to address the multi-dimensional needs of returning citizens, and what gaps exist in service delivery?
Outcomes: We hope to develop an understanding of service gaps for returning citizens and determining avenues to address them.
Resources: We can offer needs assessment, service map, partnership spreadsheet, expertise on client experiences, and Mayor’s Office networks.
Expertise: We seek expertise in criminal justice, social justice, and organizational impact on communities.

Title: Monitoring Language Access Compliance
Presenter Title: Office of Language & Communications Access
Background Info: The Office of Language & Communications Access (OLCA) will pilot a secret shopper program to evaluate spoken language interpretation services for multilingual residents seeking City resources. The pilot will focus on front-facing departments located within City Hall. Volunteers will pose as multilingual residents seeking City resources, both in person and by phone. The goal is to provide City staff with feedback on areas where exceptional language assistance is being provided, as well as opportunities for improvement. Ultimately, OLCA aims to transform the secret shopper pilot into a sustainable compliance monitoring program that can be implemented on an ongoing, annual basis.
Question: How are our multilingual residents experiencing interpretation support in their interactions with City Hall? Which offices / departments are providing thorough resources, and which have opportunities for improvement?
Outcomes: We hope to develop a report of findings, along with remedial training to address any identified areas for improvement.
Resources: We can offer staff time, data on interpretation usage, training materials for volunteer observers, a compliance monitoring handbook, and scoring sheets for observers.
Expertise: We seek expertise in client experience evaluation, interest in language access, and access to multilingual personnel to serve as volunteer observers.

Title: Building a Brain Care Tool for Boston Residents of All Ages
Presenter Title: Director of Age-Friendly Boston, Age Strong Commission
Background Info: 45% of dementia cases can be prevented or delayed through brain-healthy habits. Using the Global Brain Care Coalition’s Brain Care Score, developed by Mass General Brigham, we aim to give residents of all ages an interactive tool that educates, tracks habits, and rewards healthy routines. Even a 4-point score increase can improve brain health and reduce memory loss. Age Strong already runs brain health education, Memory Cafes, support groups, and senior center programming, and is part of the BOLD coalition. This project advances health equity and longevity, and is a goal in the upcoming Aging in Boston plan.
Question: How can we design an accessible, interactive tool to encourage brain-healthy habits for residents of all ages?
Outcomes: We hope to learn which habits residents will adopt, whether an interactive tool motivates them, and whether small incentives like gift cards improve retention.
Resources: We can offer the Brain Care Score Card (heart health, sleep, water, exercise, nutrition, social life and learning) plus neighborhood resources.
Expertise: We seek expertise in design, health behavior change, and culturally inclusive health communications.

Title: Visualizing Resident Priorities Across Participatory Budgeting Cycles
Presenter Title: Director, Office of Participatory Budgeting
Background Info: Ideas in Action, the City’s Participatory Budgeting (PB) initiative, was launched in 2024 and allows residents to directly how to use $2M of the City’s budget to benefit their communities. Each PB cycle, residents can submit ideas, draft proposals, and vote on their favorite projects to get funded. The data collected every year is a snapshot of residents’ needs and priorities, and we want to present this information back to residents, City leaders, and departmental staff in a way that can help inform future budget conversations and investments. This Dashboard was created earlier in the process, and we believe it can be improved so it becomes a more helpful resource for those involved in the budgeting process.
Question: What’s the best way to present resident priorities so that they can help inform where funding should be prioritized?
Outcomes: We hope to develop a modern, user-friendly website that allows visitors to explore the various resident ideas and themes that emerge each PB cycle, as well as a long-term tracker of consistent priorities / needs over time.
Resources: We can offer datasets from the past three PB cycles.
Expertise: We seek expertise in web and user design, programing, and LLMs.

Title: Evaluating Impact of Containerization on Rodent Populations
Presenter Title: Mayor’s Office Operations Team
Background Info: The Boston Rodent Action Plan brings together the Boston Housing Authority, Analytics, PWD Waste Reduction, Inspectional Services and Parks. Together, these departments want to test whether improved trash storage through containerization reduces rodent activity. Two pilots are proposed: containerization innovation at BHA Commonwealth, and new trash barrels in City parks. At each site, the team would measure rodent activity before and after the new containers are installed.
Question: Does improved trash storage through containerization decrease rodent activity, and which type of container has the greatest impact?
Outcomes: We hope to establish a baseline of rodent activity, introduce new trash containers, and compare activity before and after to identify the most effective container.
Resources: We can offer pilot sites, data-collection technology and partners in five City departments.
Expertise: We seek a data scientist with experience in AI-driven pest monitoring and urban rodent control.

Title: Using Emerging Technology to Digitize Park Asset Footprints
Presenter Title: Principal Research Analyst, Parks and Recreation Dept.
Background Info: Boston Parks and Recreation regularly needs to understand the boundaries of different park amenities for completing 3D modeling, understanding sunlight access, estimating maintenance costs, and conducting park redesigns. However, obtaining asset footprints can be a challenging and manual task. BPRD is interested in exploring what cutting-edge machine learning and other technologies exist for automating feature extraction of different park amenities.
Question: What machine learning tools and other technologies can be used for park feature extraction? Are the same tools well-suited to all 36 tracked assets?
Outcomes: We hope to receive a technical review of existing tools and to develop a pilot tool for testing across the park system.
Resources: We can offer staff time and expertise, networking opportunities, 10,000+ validated asset points, and various data sources (satellite imagery, layout plans).
Expertise: We seek expertise in programming, machine learning, and computer vision.

Title: Developing Measurable Water Quality Improvements at Scarboro Pond
Presenter Title: Exec. Dir. of Franklin Park, Parks and Recreation Dept.
Background Info: Franklin Park, the city’s largest public park, provides Boston hundreds of acres of park land with a diversity of uses. It is also home to Scarboro Pond, a 7.5-acre pond constructed as part of the park in 1896.  Currently, sediment and pollutants within the 300-acre watershed discharge directly into the Pond and eventually make their way into the Charles River. Nearly one-third of the runoff can be attributed to the adjacent golf course and paved areas. The Franklin Park Action Plan, published in 2022, recommends that steps be taken to evaluate inputs contributing to the pond’s poor water quality and develop measures to improve it, including invasive species management and dredging.
Question: What are critical methods to assess and improve water quality in Scarboro Pond?
Outcomes: We hope to implement measurable, low-cost operational strategies and other interventions that will systematically improve water quality in Scarboro Pond.
Resources: We can offer access to historical plans, studies, master plans. We can also facilitate discussions with our Urban Wilds Team and Conservation Commission Agents.
Expertise: We seek an ecologist with experience in natural pond and localized watershed best management practices.

Title: Monitoring Tree Health in Boston
Presenter Title: Interim Chief of Staff, Department of Innovation and Technology; Director of Urban Forestry, Boston Parks and Recreation
Background Info: Urban Forestry is an effective way of combating heat islands and extreme heat in cities. Trees help provide shade, lowering temperatures. They also improve air quality, mitigate water levels, and make neighborhoods livelier. Every year Boston plants new trees, but a certain amount do not survive, whether from storm damage, disease, pests, or failure to establish roots as young trees. Lost trees are lost investments. Can we find ways to use tree health data for City arborists to protect our investment?
Question: How healthy are our trees? Can we proactively protect the investment we already have?
Outcomes: We hope to develop a real-time map about tree needs, which arborists can use to foster better growth.
Resources: We can offer a map of all the trees in the City and staff time in developing UX/UI.
Expertise: We seek expertise in IoT sensors and the best ways to implement them into the trees / soil effectively.

Title: Developing Urban Agriculture and Climate Change Curriculum
Presenter Title: Development Officer, GrowBoston & Mayor’s Office of Housing
Background Info: GrowBoston’s goal is to increase food production and support local food producers in Boston. The impacts of climate change present a variety of increasing challenges to the ongoing success of urban agriculture. Based on feedback from key partners in the field, GrowBoston is interested in developing curriculum for food producers—gardeners, farmers, beekeepers, and more—that highlights significant challenges that climate change poses for urban agriculture and existing best practices for mitigation and adaptation.
Question: How do we prepare growers for the challenges that climate change presents for urban agriculture in Boston?
Outcomes: We hope to develop curriculum resources that GrowBoston can utilize to educate a range of food producers on climate change risks and best practices for risk management.
Resources: We can offer staff time, information about urban agriculture in Boston, and connections to relevant agencies / organizations.
Expertise: We seek expertise in reviewing existing data and curricula on the topic and creating educational resources for this project.

Title: Characterizing the Economic Potential of Unrecovered Materials
Presenter Title: Director of Waste Policy & Planning, Public Works
Background Info: Boston's municipal collection generates ~240,000 tons/year of residential waste; only 15–20% is diverted through recycling. Current recovery value is concentrated in aluminum, HDPE, and textiles. Significant fractions, including bulky waste (e.g., furniture) and organics (e.g., food waste), remain uncharacterized in terms of market potential. The project aligns with Boston's Zero Waste Plan and its 70% diversion target by 2035, prioritizing local circularity, small-business participation, and job creation.
Question: Which materials in Boston's waste stream have market value, who constitutes the end market, and under what economic and operational conditions is their recovery viable?
Outcomes: We hope to develop an end-market demand assessment and valuation by material; process efficiencies that reduce the cost of recovery; and identification of potentially scalable, locally deployable innovation models.
Resources: We can offer tonnage data by collection stream, waste composition studies, contractor-reported commodity pricing, etc.
Expertise: We seek expertise in large-dataset analysis, computational modeling, and mixed-methods research.

Title: Enabling Equitable Access to Waste Infrastructure in High-Density Housing
Presenter Title: Zero Waste Program Manager, Public Works
Background Info: New residential buildings are frequently constructed without sufficient space for waste infrastructure, leaving inadequate room for receptacles at both floor level and the curb. This results in non-standardized waste set-outs, weak incentives for residents to recycle or compost, and greater operational inefficiencies in collection. A central concern is whether buildings allocate disposal space for each waste stream. Relevant design features include multiple chutes, dedicated dumpster space, floor-level trash rooms, and at-home solutions such as garbage disposers. Where residents lack equally convenient access to all waste streams, they have less incentive to separate recyclables / organics.
Question: What combination of design standards, requirements, and incentives can ensure equitable access to all waste streams? How does infrastructure design affect source separation and collection efficiency?
Outcomes: We hope to recommend evidence-based revisions to the City's operational design guidelines and develop a planning tool that estimates waste generation.
Resources: We can offer the City's operational design guidelines, a resident behavior study, and housing data.
Expertise: We seek expertise in urban design, architecture, and building and zoning codes, along with quantitative modeling.

Title: Neighborhood-Scale Health Impacts of Air Pollution & Extreme Heat
Presenter Title: Air Quality Project Manager, Environment Department; Senior Climate Resilience Project Manager, Office of Climate Resilience
Background Info: Compounding Climate Threats: Air pollution drives a $1.4B health burden in Boston, while extreme heat causes more deaths than all other weather phenomenon combined. Driven by climate change, both of these risks are increasing — and compounding one another. The Policy Gap: The City lacks a unified, neighborhood-scale dataset evaluating the cumulative health burdens of air pollution and extreme heat under current and future climate scenarios. This framework would serve as a repeatable baseline model—allowing the City to actively measure progress and evaluate the real-world health impacts of municipal programs, retrofits, and climate policies over time.
Question: What are the cumulative health impacts of air pollution and extreme heat across Boston’s neighborhoods, how will these burdens escalate under projected climate scenarios, and how do built-environment factors modify these risks?
Outcomes: We hope to develop a neighborhood-scale air pollution and extreme heat cumulative health impact assessment, predictive climate and risk mapping, and a built-environment vulnerability layer.
Resources: We can offer quantitative air quality and temperature data, open space inventory, and access to some health data facilitated by BPHC.
Expertise: We seek expertise in environmental epidemiology, exposure science, and climate modeling.

Title: Understanding the Impact of New Housing on Local Rents
Presenter Title: Senior Policy Advisor, Planning Department
Background Info: A common concern in Boston is that new housing developments will drive up nearby rents. Academic literature on the topic presents conflicting evidence—showing new units can lower, stabilize, or increase local rents depending on the market context and methods of measurement. We lack empirical data on how this dynamic is currently playing out in Boston. Investigating the true local impacts of new development will give policymakers, community members, and developers the evidence base needed to make informed, equitable housing decisions.
Question: How does new market-rate residential development impact local market-rate rents within Boston’s neighborhoods?
Outcomes: We hope to develop an empirical study detailing rent trajectory data, hyper-local displacement risks, and actionable policy guidance for city planners and community stakeholders.
Resources: We can offer data from a related study completed recently and existing literature.
Expertise: We seek expertise in urban policy and housing.

Title: Understanding How to Incentivize Housing Instead of Unbuilt Labs
Presenter Title: Senior Policy Advisor, Planning Department
Background Info: Boston is home to 16 million sq. ft. of lab space with another 16 million in the development pipeline. The market for lab, however, has stalled. Macroeconomic shifts and NIH funding cuts have resulted in persistently high vacancy rates, risking the viability of unbuilt projects within the pipeline. Simultaneously, Boston’s housing market remains critically supply-constrained, with an urgent need for new residential units.
Question: Can we incentivize developers to build housing instead of land-banking stalled and unbuilt lab projects. What impact would these incentives have on the existing residential development market?
Outcomes: We hope to develop a policy analysis exploring possible solutions, their risks, and implementation.
Resources: We can offer development data and industry contacts.
Expertise: We seek expertise in real estate.

Title: Analyzing the Cost of Investor-Owned Units Held Vacant
Presenter Title: Senior Policy Advisor, Planning Department
Background Info: Housing costs in Boston remain high and continue to rise. While the City of Boston has launched targeted programs to address the crisis—from bridging financing gaps to requiring affordable units in new developments—one piece of the puzzle remains unexamined: Does Boston have a “ghost apartment” problem? We need to investigate what percentage of our housing stock is held vacant by investors, quantify its impact on the housing market, and identify policy solutions to unlock these units.
Question: What percentage of our housing stock is held vacant by investors, what are the impacts of this, what are other cities doing to address this issue, and what is the viability of those policies in Boston?
Outcomes: We hope to create an analysis of vacant investment properties in Boston and a policy analysis including case studies from other cities.
Resources: We can offer DoIT and Assessing datasets.
Expertise: We seek expertise in urban policy and housing.

Title: Supporting Developers in Meeting our Climate Goals
Presenter Title: Senior Policy Advisor, Planning Department
Background Info: The City of Boston recently adopted a number of progressive climate standards for new development. Amongst these requirements is our new Net Zero Carbon Zoning (Article 37). Current conditions for development are weak. Interest rates are high, material costs are high, labor costs are high, and access to financing is becoming more and more difficult. Meanwhile, we remain in a housing crisis; we need supply. Within conditions such as this regulations that increase cost come under added scrutiny. What can we do to support needed construction while also ensuring we are continuing to address the climate crisis?
Question: How can we support developers in meeting our Net Zero Carbon requirements? What tools are available?
Outcomes: We hope to create a policy analysis exploring possible solutions and the road to implementation.
Resources: We can offer development data and developer contacts.
Expertise: We seek expertise in sustainable development, real estate, and urban policy.

Title: Leveraging Data to Direct Eviction Prevention Services
Presenter Title: Director of Innovation and Technology, Mayor’s Office of Housing
Background Info: Housing instability, eviction, and homelessness remain pressing challenges in Boston. Today, the City’s eviction prevention services mostly reach constituents who self-refer, rather than the households most at risk. The City holds extensive data, including notices to quit and eviction filings, that could identify imminently at-risk tenant households and connect them to services sooner.
Question: How can the City use its data to direct eviction prevention services to households at imminent risk, rather than relying on self-referrals?
Outcomes: We hope to develop a predictive risk score for households identified through notices to quit or eviction filings, plus a simple way to refer high-risk households to targeted services.
Resources: We can offer notice to quit and eviction filing data, as well as agency staff time.
Expertise: We seek expertise in data science and predictive modeling, research and consulting, and implementation and evaluation.

Title: Mapping Mobilities of Care: Planning a Family-Friendly Boston
Presenter Title: Senior Urban Designer, Planning Department
Background Info: The Planning Department is concluding two major public asset studies—a Citywide Needs Assessment and an open space inventory. While these studies map where services exist, they do not capture when and how residents—particularly caregivers—access them.  Traditional municipal infrastructure was designed around linear 9-to-5 commuting patterns, overlooking the trip-chaining reality of caregiving—a time-cost of social reproduction. By capturing these complex, multi-stop journeys, we can align spatial planning directly with the Mayor’s priority to make Boston a family-friendly city.
Question: How can we map and analyze caregivers' daily mobility patterns in Boston to inform equitable, family-centered urban planning that addresses unevenly distributed time-costs and their intersecting impacts on employment access, housing, and more.
Outcomes: We hope to develop a report documenting caregiver journey maps and actionable urban design recommendations.
Resources: We can offer data from Citywide Needs Assessment and open space inventory, GIS / mapping assets, and MBTA trip data.
Expertise: We seek expertise in qualitative and quantitative urban research and familiarity with literature on gender and care as it relates to urban planning.

Title: Co-Creating Boston’s Family-Friendly Vision with BPS Students
Presenter Title: Senior Planner, Planning Department; Director of the Mayor's Office of Early Childhood
Background Info: The Planning Department recently begun developing a Family-Friendly City planning framework and an accompanying children’s activity book. Success depends on getting this conversation into every community. Our department currently runs a successful Planning Academy for adults and older teens, but we lack a way to engage elementary and middle school students. This project explores creating a district-wide "design sprint curriculum" focused on how to make Boston a family-friendly city. By collaborating on a focused, interactive unit with Boston Public Schools, we can empower students to envision, discuss, and shape the future of their city.
Question: How might we empower BPS students in shaping a family-friendly Boston through a hands-on design sprint?
Outcomes: We hope to develop a hands-on innovation unit and student engagement materials, a small-scale pilot workshop, and a strategy to scale the curriculum across BPS.
Resources: We can offer drafts of the Family-Friendly City vision document and children’s book, direct contacts within BPS and the Planning Department, and Planning Academy materials
Expertise: We seek expertise in K–12 curriculum design, educational campaign strategy, and youth civic engagement.

Title: Reclaiming Residential Streets for Safe Play
Presenter Name: Andrea Baena & Caroline Filice Smith, PhD
Presenter Title: Planning Department
Background Info: Residential streets were once safe spaces for neighborhood children to play and build community, but increasing car traffic has rendered many of our streets unsafe. In alignment with Boston’s Family-Friendly vision, this project seeks innovative solutions to reduce cut-through traffic in residential neighborhoods. By engaging navigation platforms like Google Maps, can we redirect commuter traffic to arterial corridors, reclaiming quiet neighborhood streets as safe, play-friendly spaces for children and families?
Question: How can the city leverage navigation platform algorithms to divert commuter cut-through traffic away from residential streets?
Outcomes: We hope to develop a pilot digital mitigation strategy for target streets and a recommended roadmap for partnership navigation platforms like Google.
Resources: We can offer GIS street network layers and city transportation contacts.
Expertise: We seek expertise in civic technology and public-private partnerships.

Title: Measuring and Mitigating Transit Pollution Exposure
Presenter Name: Caroline Filice Smith, PhD & Tori Hass-Mitchell, PhD
Presenter Title: Senior Urban Designer, Planning Department; Air Quality Project Manager, Environment Department
Background Info: Public transit is the backbone of a family-friendly city. Children and teens use it to get to school, see friends, and get to work. And families use it to navigate daily routines. When young people wait for the bus, however, they are placed adjacent to active sources of pollution. The impacts are serious. Air pollution poses measurable developmental risks for children and young people—impacting everything from educational outcomes to cardiovascular health and asthma. We do not currently know the levels of exposure faced by children in our city waiting for the bus.
Question: What levels of exposure do children and pregnant people face while waiting for the bus in Boston? When air quality is poor, what types of interventions can we test?
Outcomes: We hope to develop an understanding of air quality at bus stops around the city and intervention prototypes that work with a range of transit infrastructure (shelters, signed stops).
Resources: We can offer bus stop location data, contacts within the MBTA and Streets cabinet, and collaboration with our Air Quality program manager in Environment.
Expertise: We seek expertise in air quality sensing and prototyping.

Title: Developing an Interactive Guide to Construction Costs
Presenter Title: Senior Urban Designer, Planning Department
Background Info: There is a widespread lack of knowledge around what it actually costs to build in Boston. A common perception is that escalating housing prices are driven primarily by developer profits. Building on the Planning Department’s Planning Academy initiative—a planning school for residents—this project seeks to create an interactive tool that breaks down the true anatomy of construction expenses. By visualizing the costs of financing and building in our city, the tool will illuminate the "floor" of development costs—the minimum price threshold before any developer profit—replacing speculation with transparency and fostering informed, constructive policy dialogues across Boston.
Question: What is the cost-floor of residential construction in Boston, where do those costs originate, and how can an interactive tool clarify the economic realities of development for the public and decision-makers? Is there a data collection process that would allow us to keep this information up to date?
Outcomes: We hope to develop an interactive storytelling web tool detailing costs across labor, materials, permitting, and financing.
Resources: We can offer affordable housing cost data from MoH, local developer contacts, and Multifamily Guidebook data.
Expertise: We seek expertise in real estate and construction, housing, UX, and urban studies.

Title: Building a Comprehensive Business Intelligence & Mobility Data Foundation
Presenter Title: Senior Economist, Planning Department: Research Division
Background Info: Boston’s Research Division needs a reliable picture of the city’s business ecosystem to support business attraction, retention, and expansion. Public datasets provide limited establishment counts, broad industries, and employment ranges, while commercial datasets can contain inactive businesses, inaccurate addresses, and limited information about relocations. We have explored sources and reconciliation methods, but a gap remains: • We cannot identify every active Boston business or understand its characteristics and movement. • Tax filing data from the Department of Revenue could provide a foundation, if a qualified research partner can access and analyze confidential records.
Question: Can confidential tax filing data establish a reliable business baseline and reveal where businesses originate, relocate, and leave?
Outcomes: We hope to develop a validated methodology and business profile covering counts, locations, industries, employment, revenue, and mobility patterns.
Resources: We can offer existing datasets, analytical work, and City expertise.
Expertise: We seek a partner that has established, or can establish, authorized access to confidential DOR data. The Division has been unable to obtain the data directly. The partner should also have expertise in administrative data, business dynamics, record linkage, and economic analysis.

Title: Scaling Rental Registration Compliance via Earlier Identification
Presenter Title: Inspectional Services Department
Background Info: Rental Registration helps ISD identify rental properties for oversight and enforcement. Approximately 75% of units in the rental universe comply with the ordinance. The remaining units are unregistered.  Today, identifying units that should enter the Rental Registry relies on owner self-reporting or manual identification by inspectors. ISD wants to test whether existing City data can identify eligible properties earlier and create a reliable path for registration follow-up.
Question: How can ISD identify units subject to the Rental Registry ordinance as soon as they come online? Can Certificate of Occupancy trigger a referral to Housing for eligibility review?
Outcomes: We hope to develop a tested referral method, eligibility and data-matching rules, and a tracking prototype that measures eligible units identified, time from CO to review, registration outcomes, and unresolved cases.
Resources: We can offer records (CO, Rental Registration and property), City systems, and staff time.
Expertise: We seek expertise in workflow design, data matching, digital prototyping, and pilot evaluation.

Title: Strengthening Housing Complaint Follow-Up
Presenter Title: Acting Director of Housing, Inspectional Services Department
Background Info: Residents submit housing complaints through several channels. Staff coordinate intake, inspections and follow-up across email and case systems to address housing conditions. Experienced staff keep work moving through personal review and coordination. Their knowledge offers a starting point for documenting handoffs and making pending actions easier to see. Early observations suggest an opportunity to reduce manual coordination. Staff would validate the workflow and define a pilot that supports consistent follow-up.
Question: How can Housing capture staff expertise in a shared complaint workflow that makes case ownership and follow-up visible while reducing manual coordination?
Outcomes: We hope to develop a documented workflow and tracker for one complaint pathway, with staff-defined follow-up rules and measurement of assignment time, manual status checks, and missing next actions.
Resources: We can offer sample complaint records, process documentation, and staff interviews.
Expertise: We seek expertise in service design, workflow research, case-system analysis, and digital prototyping.

Title: Increasing Family Engagement with Boston Saves
Presenter Title: Program Director, Worker Empowerment Cabinet
Background Info: Boston Saves is the City of Boston’s children’s savings account program. Each year, the K2 students in Boston Public Schools receive a Boston Saves account with an initial $50 and can earn additional incentives by engaging in savings and age-appropriate reading, career exploration, and financial education activities. The program now has 24,000+ active accounts across 95 schools, yet only about 36% of families actively engage. We have years of program data. We want to better understand what drives engagement—and what we can change to increase it.
Question: What factors drive family engagement with Boston Saves, and what interventions could increase participation?
Outcomes: We hope to identify patterns in engagement and develop 3–5 actionable strategies that Boston Saves can test.
Resources: We can offer program data on account engagement, incentives, savings activity, schools and grade levels, plus outreach materials and staff expertise.
Expertise: We seek expertise in program evaluation, behavioral science, data analysis, and/or human-centered design.

Title: Developing a Public-Facing Tool for Occupational Trends & AI Exposure
Presenter Title: Data Analyst & Learning Specialist, Worker Empowerment Cabinet
Background Info: Workers and local residents navigate a complex career development process, made increasingly unpredictable by the effects of AI on the labor market. The public seeks resources and tools to help understand this landscape, and given the local nature of job markets, the City of Boston is in position to be a resource. We want to develop a public-facing tool that users can utilize to understand occupational projections and trends in the Boston area. This data would include occupational growth, wages, and estimates of AI exposure, as well as information on local training programs and top employers.
Question: How can the City provide a public tool that accurately and succinctly communicates occupational labor market data to job seekers?
Outcomes: We hope to produce a minimum viable product that will provide the public with information to make informed career decisions.
Resources: We can offer staff time, public and internal data, and local job training information.
Expertise: We seek expertise in data management and building digital tools, as well as workforce domain knowledge.
